name: Conk

lead: The conk is a hairstyle made by chemically straightening naturally kinky or curly hair so it lies smooth and can be combed into waves, slicked back or lifted into a pompadour. It was especially popular among African American men from the 1920s to the mid-1960s, with a glossy finish as part of the look.

Its appearance payoff is straight, sleek, styleable hair from textured hair. It has also been discussed in cultural terms, as a symbol of assimilation in some accounts and later criticised during the rise of the Black Power and natural hair movements.

paras: Historically the straightening used strong alkaline (lye-based) relaxer mixtures that break the hair's disulfide bonds, followed by rinsing, neutralising and styling with pomade. Modern hair relaxers include lye and no-lye types, and professionals apply them. This article does not give preparation instructions.

Chemical relaxers are listed as causing chemical burns and hair breakage, and the original lye mixtures were notorious for painful scalp burns. Wikipedia also notes that some relaxers contain formaldehyde-releasing agents that a 2017 study linked to higher breast cancer risk.

chain: Smooth hair can be waved, slicked or raised into a pompadour
angle.text: The straightening changes the hair's texture so it can be shaped into styles that tight curls cannot easily hold. The result is a sleek, shiny finish that lasts until new growth emerges.

lead: The conk is a hairstyle in which naturally kinky or coily hair is chemically straightened and styled into a smooth, glossy form, often a pompadour, waves or a slicked-back style [1]. It gained prominence among African American men in the United States and was popular from the 1920s until the mid-1960s, especially in jazz and entertainment scenes [1].

Straightened hair was achieved with a lye-based relaxer, commonly sold or homemade, that could cause intense burning on the scalp [1]. Wikipedia's article on hair straightening explains that relaxers work by breaking the hair's disulfide bonds, that lye relaxers contain sodium hydroxide while non-lye relaxers use calcium hydroxide and suit more sensitive scalps, and that chemical burns and hair breakage are listed risks [2].

The style has been interpreted in several ways. Some accounts describe it as an effort to meet mainstream beauty norms for social and professional advancement, and note a backlash during the rise of the Black Power movement and natural hair advocacy, with Malcolm X among those who wrote about it in his memoir [1]. Looksmaxxing communities mention it as a style that gives hair volume and a slicked shape.

paras: The conk changes naturally kinky or curly hair into a smooth, malleable form that can be waved, slicked or lifted for height [1]. Hair that is treated this way looks glossy once rinsed, neutralised and set with pomade [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, contrasts it with temporary hot-comb pressing, which wears off with shampooing, while chemical straightening lasts until new growth emerges [1].

Hot combs and relaxers have a long history among African American men and women; Wikipedia notes that Madam C. J. Walker popularised the straightening comb in the early 1900s although she did not invent it, and that her system emphasised hygiene and scalp health [2]. The conk rose in popularity through the 1920s and declined in the late 1960s as afros and chemical-free textures became popular [1]. Malcolm X described the experience in his autobiography [1].

The lye-based mixtures used for conking were corrosive and risked severe scalp burns [1]. Wikipedia lists chemical burns and hair breakage as risks of chemical straightening and notes that some products contain formaldehyde-releasing agents linked in a 2017 study to higher breast cancer risk [2]. Non-lye relaxers are described as suitable for more sensitive scalps [2].

timeline.event: Madam C. J. Walker popularises the straightening comb [2].
The conk becomes prominent among African American men [1].
The conk declines as afros and natural textures gain prominence [1].
